[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Garbage Collection in Python"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Garbage collection is a crucial automatic memory management feature in Python. It reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use, preventing memory leaks and ensuring efficient resource utilization. Python's garbage collector primarily uses two techniques: reference counting and generational garbage collection."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Reference Counting"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Reference counting is the primary garbage collection mechanism in Python. Every object maintains a reference count, which tracks the number of references pointing to it. When an object's reference count drops to zero, it means the object is no longer accessible and can be safely deallocated."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"# Example demonstrating reference counting
import sys

a = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # Output: 2 (one from 'a', one from getrefcount())

b = a
print(sys.getrefcount(a))  # Output: 3 (one from 'a', one from 'b', one from getrefcount())

del a
print(sys.getrefcount(b))  # Output: 2 (one from 'b', one from getrefcount())

del b
# Object is now garbage collected"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'sys.getrefcount()' function can be used to check the reference count of an object. Note that calling 'sys.getrefcount()' itself increases the reference count temporarily."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Generational Garbage Collection"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"While reference counting is effective for many objects, it fails to collect objects involved in circular references (where two or more objects refer to each other). To address this, Python employs a generational garbage collector."},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The generational garbage collector categorizes objects into generations based on their age (how long they have survived). It assumes that younger objects are more likely to become garbage than older ones. Therefore, it focuses on collecting younger generations more frequently."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Python's garbage collector has three generations (0, 1, and 2). Generation 0 is the youngest, and generation 2 is the oldest. When the number of allocations minus the number of deallocations exceeds a certain threshold, the garbage collector runs on that generation."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"import gc

# Check if the garbage collector is enabled
print(gc.isenabled())

# Manually trigger garbage collection
gc.collect()

# Get the current garbage collection thresholds
print(gc.get_threshold())

# Set the garbage collection thresholds
gc.set_threshold(700, 10, 10) # (threshold0, threshold1, threshold2)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The 'gc' module provides functions to interact with the garbage collector. 'gc.isenabled()' checks if the garbage collector is enabled. 'gc.collect()' manually triggers a garbage collection cycle. 'gc.get_threshold()' returns the current collection thresholds for the generations, and 'gc.set_threshold()' allows you to modify these thresholds. The thresholds determine how often each generation is collected."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Circular References"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Circular references occur when two or more objects refer to each other, creating a cycle. Reference counting alone cannot detect these cycles because the reference counts of the objects involved will never reach zero, even if they are no longer accessible from the rest of the program."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"# Example of circular references
import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.next = None

# Create two nodes with a circular reference
a = Node(1)
b = Node(2)
a.next = b
b.next = a

# Delete the references to the nodes
del a
del b

# Manually trigger garbage collection
print(gc.collect())
# The garbage collector will break the cycle and reclaim the memory."},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the example above, nodes 'a' and 'b' form a circular reference. Even after deleting the references 'a' and 'b', the nodes are still referencing each other. The generational garbage collector is responsible for detecting and breaking these cycles."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Disabling Garbage Collection"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"In some performance-critical applications, you might want to temporarily disable the garbage collector to avoid unpredictable pauses. However, this should be done with caution, as it can lead to memory leaks if not managed properly."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"import gc

# Disable garbage collection
gc.disable()

# Enable garbage collection
gc.enable()"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Use 'gc.disable()' to disable the garbage collector and 'gc.enable()' to re-enable it. Remember to re-enable the garbage collector after performing the performance-critical operations."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Python's garbage collection system, combining reference counting and generational garbage collection, provides automatic memory management, simplifying development and preventing memory-related issues. Understanding how it works allows you to write more efficient and robust Python code."}]
